Paper Title: "The bus is accessible, but how do you get to the bus": First and last mile experiences of disabled transit riders
Central claim: Disabled transit riders in Austin and Seattle face similar first and last mile barriers despite different transit systems and geographies, shaped by intersectionality, social context, built environment quality, confidence, and relationships with public agencies. Disabled voices are systematically excluded from planning, perpetuating inequitable outcomes.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility justice: multi-scalar framework examining how the built environment reproduces privilege and power beyond basic accessibility. First and last mile: trip segments connecting riders to fixed transit, where accessibility gaps concentrate. Intersectionality: overlapping identities shaping distinct travel burdens.
Who is centered: Sixteen disabled transit riders in Austin and Seattle, recruited through disability advocacy organizations, centered through first-person interview accounts.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access and flexibility for variable need: ADA compliance measures and stop-count accessibility metrics ignore first and last mile segments and diverse disability needs.
Relevance to argument: Supports both halves of the claim. Mobility access is unevenly distributed by disability type, gender, and race even in cities with strong accessibility investment, and infrastructure built to minimum ADA standards without disabled riders' participation reproduces exclusion along the first and last mile. Participants report being seldom in the room when transportation decisions are made, and describe the active transportation engagement process itself as white and male dominated.
Gap or limitation: The sample was recruited through advocacy networks and email, skewing toward riders already engaged with accessibility issues and excluding disabled people without internet access.
Quotable moment: "The bus is accessible, but how do you get to the bus?" (p. 5).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds both the uneven distribution and exclusion-from-participation claims in first-person accounts, showing that even accessibility-focused cities produce disproportionate travel burdens when planners ignore first and last mile segments and exclude disabled riders from decision-making. It argues meaningful engagement, not compliance alone, is necessary for equitable mobility infrastructure.
Codesign/participatory method: Semi-structured qualitative interviews with 16 disabled transit riders in Austin and Seattle (Sept to Dec 2022), recruited via purposive and snowball sampling through disability and transit advocacy organizations, community centers, and agency advisory committees. Interviews ran 30 to 60 minutes over Zoom, were transcribed and inductively coded with peer reviewed reliability checks. Consultative research design that elicits lived experience testimony for the author's own analysis, not a process giving participants decision making authority.
What worked: Recruiting through established disability advocacy organizations and agency advisory committees reached participants already embedded in first and last mile issues and yielded rich testimony. Flexible virtual scheduling and letting participants self identify their disability rather than sorting them into researcher defined categories surfaced experiences standard categories miss (p. 4).
What didn't work: The author acknowledges recruiting through advocacy networks and email skewed the sample toward already engaged, more aware individuals and excluded disabled people without internet access (p. 4). Participants also described agency led engagement pilots that solicited community input and co-creation but went silent afterward, one saying of a transit pilot, "you hear nothing" once it ended (p. 6).

Paper Title: Public transport inclusion and active aging: A systematic review on elderly mobility
Journal or Proceedings: Journal of Traffic and Transportation Engineering (English Edition), 11(2), 312-347
Central claim: A systematic review of 138 papers finds the elderly experience the highest inequality in public transport resource distribution among disadvantaged traveler groups. It synthesizes a four part framework, opportunity accessibility, physical accessibility, age friendly informationalization, and cost affordability, for transport inclusion policy.
Key concepts or framework: Transport related social exclusion: marginalization from daily activities caused by inadequate transport across accessibility, physical, information, and economic dimensions. Capability approach: evaluates inclusion by whether services convert into real capabilities. Spatial production theory: transport spaces shape perceived social inclusion.
Who is centered: The perspective of transport planners and policymakers, synthesized through published research rather than elderly travelers' own accounts.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust and flexibility for variable need: the framework measures inclusion through accessibility and cost metrics rather than relationships or elderly travelers' own participation in defining inclusion.
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half directly, documenting that elderly people face the highest transport resource inequality among disadvantaged groups across three decades of research. It does not address community participation in infrastructure decisions: its own framework is top down and metric driven, built from published literature rather than elderly travelers' input, making it a thinner fit for the infrastructure without participation half of the claim.
Gap or limitation: The evaluation framework assumes public transit dependent cities and fits poorly in car dependent or rural contexts, and it pools evidence on other disadvantaged groups without a participatory method to test the framework directly.
Quotable moment: "the elderly have the highest level of inequality in PT resource distribution" (p. 2).
Synthesis paragraph: This review documents that elderly people face the steepest transport inequality among disadvantaged groups, giving quantitative backing to the claim that mobility access has long been unevenly distributed. Its own accessibility centered framework, however, is built from literature rather than elderly voices, illustrating by contrast why participatory approaches matter for defining what inclusion requires.
Codesign/participatory method: None described. This is a top down synthesis of 138 published studies rather than the authors' own fieldwork; it notes in passing that some reviewed studies used focus groups or in depth interviews as a data collection method, but gives no detail on who was involved, how, or with what outcome.
What worked: N/A
What didn't work: N/A

Paper Title: Bridging the gap: Do community needs assessments enhance public participation in transportation planning?
Central claim: California's community transportation needs assessment pilot program, intended to include historically underrepresented groups in transportation planning, largely reproduced the same representation gaps and engagement shortfalls as traditional public participation processes.
Key concepts or framework: Community transportation needs assessment: a grassroots funded study meant to engage underrepresented residents in identifying transportation needs. Representation gap: participants in planning processes skew older, whiter, and more affluent than the community. Tokenism: participation that solicits input without incorporating it into decisions.
Who is centered: Local organizations and residents surveyed under California's Clean Mobility Options pilot, analyzed through awardees' final reports and survey data rather than participant narratives.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access: even purpose built participatory processes struggled to reach disadvantaged and hard to reach populations, leaving the same groups underrepresented as in conventional public meetings.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half of the claim. It shows that even funded, explicitly inclusive community needs assessments replicate historic representation gaps rather than closing them, and traces this pattern back to the 1950s and 1960s highway projects that displaced low income and Black residents with little say in the process.
Gap or limitation: The study cannot confirm whether any assessment's recommendations changed actual transportation plans or funding, and it analyzes only California's pilot program, limiting generalizability to other participatory models.
Quotable moment: "urban renewal projects of the 1950s and 1960s that displaced more than 1 million Americans, residents that were disproportionately low-income and Black" (p. 2).
Synthesis paragraph: Even when agencies fund grassroots, explicitly inclusive needs assessments, this study finds they largely reproduce the same representation gaps as traditional public meetings. It underscores that participation structures, not just their existence, determine whether infrastructure decisions genuinely include disadvantaged communities, grounding the section's exclusion claim in a contemporary case rather than only historical precedent.
Codesign/participatory method: Secondary comparative analysis, not the authors' own fieldwork, of five California Clean Mobility Options community transportation needs assessment awardees' final reports and survey data, benchmarked against long range transportation plans' public participation records. Awardees used varied methods: surveys, workshops, focus groups, interviews, community meetings, stakeholder phone calls, photovoice, collaborative mapping, and one virtual reality component, often co hosted with community based organizations. The authors evaluate whether these funded, explicitly inclusive processes reached and empowered underrepresented residents, not whether their own study did.
What worked: Awardees that met residents where they already gathered, such as churches, food distribution lines, or parent nights, and organizations with pre-existing trust or ties to community groups generated stronger turnout than cold outreach. Hiring local staff, using experienced consultants, and targeting small, tightly networked populations like tribes improved response and demographic reach. A consultant on staff nearly tripled the population adjusted response rate (p. 5-6).
What didn't work: Snowball sampling and mailed flyers mostly reached people already engaged, and events requiring travel or extra time suppressed turnout even when reach was high. Awardees rarely tracked participant demographics, especially for focus groups and interviews, so several could not confirm representativeness. One awardee's own report admitted its focus group participants "appeared to be primarily white and older" despite not collecting that data (p. 6). Targeted groups like unemployed or youth residents stayed underrepresented regardless of method.

Paper Title: Moving Towards Mobility Justice: Challenges and Considerations for Supporting Advocacy
Central claim: Interviews with Canadian transportation advocates identify four ways that mobility planning tools and information systems deepen the divide between planners and the public. Path dependence in transportation knowledge infrastructures is a systemic barrier to overcoming these mobility injustices.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility justice: Sheller's framework analyzing interacting relations of movement, dividing populations into kinetic elite and mobility poor. Path dependence: how the historical design of planning tools locks in and perpetuates exclusion. Data infrastructure literacy: sensitivity to the social and political contexts data is embedded in.
Who is centered: Mobility justice advocates and community organizers across Canada, centered through their own accounts of interacting with planning technologies and processes.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access and relational trust: technical, jargon heavy planning tools and English only materials exclude non expert and non English speaking residents from decisions imposed on them.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. Advocates describe how technically inaccessible tools, English only materials, and planners' hyper focus on traffic counts over lived experience shut residents out of decisions, echoing the historical divide between the kinetic elite and the mobility poor that mobility justice scholarship names.
Gap or limitation: The sample is limited to advocacy organizations already engaged in mobility justice work in Canada, so it may not capture residents who never reach an advocacy organization at all.
Quotable moment: "a conversation that only some people are allowed to be in" (p. 8).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds the exclusion half of the claim in current advocacy work, showing that technical jargon, English only materials, and planners' narrow traffic metrics reproduce the same divide between decision makers and residents that mobility justice scholarship critiques historically. It introduces path dependence as a mechanism for why exclusionary infrastructure persists.
Codesign/participatory method: The authors' own method is 16 semi-structured interviews with senior figures at Canadian mobility justice organizations, recruited via civic technology groups, snowball sampling, and personal contacts between June and September 2022, conducted over Zoom, 45 to 60 minutes, analyzed via two coder reflective thematic analysis. Substantively, interviewees describe two separate participatory practices as their advocacy subject matter: municipal public participation via city planning meetings and town halls, and advocacy led community outreach such as temporary pop up demonstrations. These are the interviewees' accounts of processes the authors did not run themselves.
What worked: Advocacy organizations' own outreach, not the cities', is what interviewees describe succeeding. Temporary pop up demonstrations of mobility solutions paired with deliberate storytelling messaging that frames changes as a reversible pilot built resident buy in and reduced resistance to proposed changes (p. 8).
What didn't work: Interviewees describe municipal public participation through city planning meetings and town halls as excluding residents through technical, jargon heavy proposals, with one advocate calling it "a conversation that only some people are allowed to be in" (p. 8). Everyday transit information and outreach materials being English only, despite roughly 50 languages spoken in Toronto, further shut out non-English speaking riders from participating (p. 8).

Paper Title: Co-Creating Accessibility-Centred Mobility Strategies in Low-Density Suburban Contexts: Evidence from Coimbra, Portugal
Central claim: Three co-creation focus groups with institutional, technical, and citizen actors in a low-density Portuguese suburb produced eight collaboratively defined mobility strategies spanning pedestrian and cycling infrastructure, transit reliability, and governance. Accessibility, inclusiveness, and institutional coordination emerge as interdependent conditions for equitable mobility transitions.
Key concepts or framework: 15-Minute City, Transit-Oriented Development, and Mobility as a Service: proximity based planning paradigms reinterpreted by participants as functional access goals rather than fixed density templates. Co-creation: focus group based collective strategy building across institutional, technical, and citizen stakeholders.
Who is centered: Institutional, technical, and citizen actors in Sao Martinho do Bispo, a low-density Coimbra suburb, though citizen participants were predominantly older adults.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Flexibility for variable need: participants were predominantly older adults, so younger low-income residents, migrants, and people with disabilities were underrepresented in shaping the co-created strategies.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, showing that treating proximity-based models like the 15-Minute City and TOD as co-created rather than fixed templates surfaces needs, such as trust in transit reliability and safe pedestrian access, that top down planning alone would miss.
Gap or limitation: The case draws on a single suburb and a limited number of focus groups skewed toward older participants, so the strategies are preliminary and unvalidated against underrepresented groups' needs.
Quotable moment: "key to rebuilding trust in public transport" (p. 22).
Synthesis paragraph: This case shows that participatory reinterpretation of proximity based planning models, rather than top down application, is what surfaces suburban residents' actual priorities, though the strategies here reflect mostly older adults and remain unvalidated. It offers a concrete example of co-creation as a mechanism for avoiding exclusionary infrastructure.
Codesign/participatory method: Three deliberative focus groups in Sao Martinho do Bispo, Coimbra (March to April 2025) with 18 institutional, technical, and citizen participants, recruited through local associations, municipal contacts, and institutional partnerships. Institutional and citizen stakeholders met in separate sessions to reduce power asymmetries. A four phase structure moved from trust building to mapping priorities, generating individual proposals, and collectively assessing and co creating eight territorial strategies. Sessions were recorded, transcribed, and analyzed with co-occurrence coding. Consultative and advisory: the co created strategies are framed as preliminary inputs needing further validation, not binding decisions.
What worked: Separating institutional/technical and citizen groups let citizens articulate everyday constraints without institutional influence and let officials speak candidly about feasibility, reducing power asymmetries (p. 8). The structured four phase deliberation and co-design process was described as transformative, with participants moving beyond identifying barriers to collectively reframing mobility as a shared public responsibility (p. 24).
What didn't work: Citizen participants skewed toward older adults reflecting the area's demographics, likely underrepresenting younger, low income, migrant, or disabled residents. Recruitment was also constrained by limited availability and willingness to participate in this car dependent suburb (p. 27). The authors caution that subtle institutional framing was not fully eliminated despite group separation, and the co created strategies remain unvalidated proposals, not implementation commitments (p. 27).

Paper Title: Toward Structured Public Involvement: Justice, Geography and Collaborative Geospatial/Geovisual Decision Support Systems
Journal or Proceedings: Annals of the Association of American Geographers, 100(1), 57-86
Central claim: Surveys of transportation professionals and the public reveal an Arnstein Gap, a persistent difference between the public involvement stakeholders experience and what they want in transportation infrastructure planning. The paper proposes structured public involvement, using geovisual decision support tools, to narrow this gap without requiring full consensus.
Key concepts or framework: Arnstein Gap: the measured difference between perceived and desired public involvement on Arnstein's ladder of citizen participation. Structured public involvement: a reflexive, nonconsensual framework using geovisual tools to elicit and respect community cultural values. Procedural justice: attaining spatial justice through fair process rather than fair distribution alone.
Who is centered: Transportation professionals and public stakeholders surveyed across Kentucky, Indiana, Arizona, and Alaska, compared to reveal gaps in perceived versus desired involvement.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust: surveyed professionals showed a professional conceit, believing public involvement worked better than the public itself reported, reflecting distrust that constrains genuine collaboration.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. The Arnstein Gap quantifies a persistent, measured shortfall in transportation infrastructure decision making that professionals do not fully recognize, and the paper argues this gap is structural to U.S. transportation planning rather than an occasional failure.
Gap or limitation: The survey based Arnstein Gap metric captures perceived involvement levels but not whether structured public involvement deployments change actual infrastructure outcomes, and the case studies are limited to a handful of U.S. states.
Quotable moment: "The Arnstein Gap indicates that the public desire a TI planning and design system that is more directly responsive to public needs" (p. 7).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers historical and methodological grounding for why participation gaps in infrastructure planning persist, showing empirically that professionals underestimate the disconnect between desired and actual public involvement. It supports treating infrastructure without participation as a structural, measurable problem, and frames a participatory alternative that need not require full consensus to be legitimate.
Codesign/participatory method: Reviews two of the authors' own structured public involvement (SPI) case studies embedded within standard public meetings on U.S. highway projects, up to 300 attendees per event. AMIS is a facilitated GIS and multicriteria corridor evaluation eliciting stakeholder impedance values for landscape features via focus group meetings and AHP weighting, applied to a Kentucky highway corridor. CAVE is a fuzzy logic Likert scale visual preference survey scoring twenty to thirty design visualizations per two hour session, applied to noise wall and bridge design. Anonymous, simultaneous, one person one input scoring reduces strategic behavior, framed as consultative input into decisions agencies still make.
What worked: Anonymous input collection surfaced concerns officials did not know existed. A Kentucky caving group's data on cave locations and recreational value, gathered confidentially through AMIS, reshaped the corridor route once engineers saw it (p. 18). SPI fit inside existing public meetings rather than requiring extra ones, which lowered sponsors' and professionals' resistance to adopting it and let large crowds participate on equal footing (p. 23).
What didn't work: The research team never held direct power to guarantee designs got built, and performance still partly reflected each project sponsor's preferred Arnstein Ladder position, meaning agencies could still limit how much influence input carried (p. 23). CAVE's format caps meetings at roughly twenty to thirty scoreable images in two hours, too few for reliable statistical analysis, and the authors concede SPI does not resolve whether attendees are a representative sample of the public (p. 19, 23).

Paper Title: Centering disability justice in active transportation transitions: A conceptual counter-cartography
Central claim: Twenty interviews with disabled people in Montreal and a conceptual counter-cartography approach show that dominant definitions of active travel, limited to biking and walking on foot, exclude wheelchair, scooter, and adapted cycle users. The paper argues infrastructure should center disability justice and disabled people's leadership rather than retrofit universal design standards.
Key concepts or framework: Counter-cartography: a mapping method layering policy definitions against interview accounts to expose whose mobility practices get excluded. Disability justice: a framework centering disabled people's leadership, distinct from accommodation focused universal design. Crip time: reframing infrastructure to bend to disabled bodies' pace rather than the reverse.
Who is centered: Twenty people with disabilities in Montreal, interviewed about their own active travel practices and infrastructure needs.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Flexibility for variable need: Montreal's official definitions of active travel as biking or walking on foot formally exclude wheelchairs, scooters, and adapted cycles from infrastructure meant to serve them.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. Montreal's own policy definitions of active travel exclude many disabled people's actual mobility practices, and interviewees describe cycling infrastructure too narrow for tricycles and adapted cycles, showing how planning built without disabled people's input structurally forecloses their access.
Gap or limitation: The study draws on 20 interviews in a single city, and the authors call for broader research across more disability communities to inform infrastructural design processes.
Quotable moment: "sidewalks hit hard" (p. 6).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper shows that official definitions of active travel, not just physical infrastructure, can foreclose disabled people's access, since Montreal's own policy language excludes many disabled mobility practices before infrastructure is even built. It reinforces that centering disabled people's expertise and leadership, not only accommodation, is necessary for genuinely inclusive infrastructure decisions.
Codesign/participatory method: The authors' own conceptual counter-cartography method is explicitly participatory: people with disabilities and Quebec disability organizations helped choose methods, design research tools, shape recruitment, and analyze data, not just serve as interview subjects. Core data comes from 20 semi-structured, one to two hour interviews with disabled Montrealers, recruited via stratified purposeful sampling through partner organizations, covering local transportation experiences and public consultation processes, paired with analysis of 15 local active transportation and accessibility policies. Interviewees separately described the city's own public consultation forums for active transportation planning.
What worked: Recruiting through disability partner organizations who helped design the study, not just supply participants, produced a sample spanning a range of disability types, ages, and 11 of Montreal's 19 boroughs. Many interviewees credited the city's cycling network expansion itself as a genuine effort responding to community pressure, even while critiquing its design (p. 4).
What didn't work: The authors could not meaningfully include people with intellectual disabilities within this study's methods and are addressing that gap through a separate, adapted participatory project, calling it a key limitation of the findings reported here (p. 4). Interviewees also reported a broader lack of appropriate participation modalities, and of accountability for social inclusion commitments, within Montreal's technical and public consultation forums for transportation planning (p. 5).

Paper Title: Performative versus Authentic Equity Work: An Assessment of Current Practices in Transportation Planning
Central claim: Interviews with 28 Black and people of color transportation professionals in California distinguish performative equity work, which privileges dominant groups' comfort and produces only superficial change, from authentic equity work, which redistributes decision making power and produces measurable change for historically oppressed communities.
Key concepts or framework: Performative equity work: actions or rhetoric that claim to address equity without materially changing outcomes or power. Authentic equity work: sustained redistribution of funding, time, and decision making power to affected communities. Arrested mobility: policing practices that apprehend or harm Black people simply for moving through public space.
Who is centered: Twenty eight California transportation professionals who identify as Black, Indigenous, or people of color, centered through their own workplace and policy experiences.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust and equitable access: performative equity work keeps decision making power concentrated among historically dominant, often white leadership, even while claiming to value equity, leaving communities without real control over resources.
Relevance to argument: Supports both halves of the claim. It documents uneven distribution of power and voice among transportation professionals of color within the field itself, and argues that infrastructure and funding decisions made without genuinely redistributing power to communities, not just consulting them, reproduce the same exclusion regardless of stated equity commitments.
Gap or limitation: The study is limited to California and did not achieve representation from Indigenous or tribal transportation professionals despite specific recruitment efforts, limiting the framework's tested scope.
Quotable moment: "Many communities know the solutions to the challenges they face" (p. 12).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper reframes community participation as insufficient unless paired with actual redistribution of power and resources, showing that even self identified equity conscious agencies can produce only performative change. It supports the section's exclusion claim by locating the same power imbalance inside the transportation profession itself, not only in public facing planning processes.
Codesign/participatory method: The authors' own method is 28 semi-structured interviews with BIPOC transportation professionals, conducted between April 2020 and 2021, recruited through referrals and thematically coded, asking how they view equity work in their agencies. Interviewees describe two contrasting community engagement models: performative outreach that checklists community input after decisions are already made, versus a Central Valley group's monthly equity led agenda meetings, where residents envision the community they want, that vision is translated into plans and policies, and organizers then advocate to get those plans implemented so residents benefit from their own feedback.
What worked: The Central Valley model's recurring monthly meetings, which fed resident visions directly into plans and then into advocacy for implementation, was cited as authentic engagement because residents saw a throughline from input to outcome, not just being heard. Interviewees also stressed that trust building takes ongoing relationships with the most neglected residents, not one time consultation (p. 11).
What didn't work: Interviewees described performative engagement as checking an outreach box or being brought in only after a project's decisions were already made, calling it a process where feedback "can't really impact much" (p. 11). One professional said real equity means removing and redistributing power, not just "being invited to the process," and several noted agencies chronically underinvest the time and resources engagement actually requires (p. 12).

Paper Title: Assessing equity in infrastructure investment distribution among U.S. cities
Central claim: A deep learning analysis of infrastructure expenditure and social vulnerability across 394 US municipalities finds infrastructure investment inequality increased from 2010 to 2019 in nearly every sector, and that shifting from population based to equity centered funding allocation would measurably reduce socioeconomic vulnerability.
Key concepts or framework: Social Vulnerability Index: a CDC composite measure of socioeconomic disadvantage used to track which municipalities are underserved. Equality centered versus equity centered allocation: distributing infrastructure funds evenly per capita versus targeting funds toward the most vulnerable municipalities.
Who is centered: The perspective of planners and policymakers modeling municipal level spending data; no residents of the municipalities studied are directly consulted.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust and flexibility for variable need: the model treats equity as a quantitative allocation formula, and the authors themselves note it lacks the community engagement needed to capture residents' actual perspectives and concerns.
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half directly, quantifying growing infrastructure investment inequality across a decade and showing which municipalities are shortchanged. It is a thinner fit for the participation half: the framework is data driven and top down, and the authors themselves flag the need to pair it with community engagement to make decisions genuinely equitable.
Gap or limitation: The model treats infrastructure categories broadly without distinguishing transportation modes, relies on a black box machine learning approach whose internal relationships are hard to interpret, and by the authors' own account still needs community-driven qualitative input.
Quotable moment: "fosters community engagement and ownership, leading to further improvements in the equitable decision-making process" (p. 11).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers strong quantitative evidence that infrastructure investment inequality has been widening and that equity centered allocation would help close it, reinforcing the section's uneven distribution claim. It is honest about its own limits, though: as a purely data driven model, it cannot substitute for the community engagement the section argues infrastructure decisions actually require.
Codesign/participatory method: None described. This is a quantitative, GIS and social vulnerability index driven framework for evaluating infrastructure investment allocation across cities. It cites other scholars (Bailey and Grossardt 2010, Karner and Marcantonio 2018) approvingly for the importance of community engagement and recommends surveys and interviews as future work, but the authors' own methodology involves no interaction with residents or communities.
What worked: N/A
What didn't work: N/A

Paper Title: Race, Space, and Struggles for Mobility: Transportation Impacts on African Americans in Oakland and the East Bay
Central claim: A 2005 civil rights lawsuit against the Bay Area's Metropolitan Transportation Commission reveals that race neutral regional transit funding, favoring suburban rail expansion over Oakland bus service, reproduced a racialized geography built by decades of earlier overt housing and employment discrimination.
Key concepts or framework: Environmental racism framework: analyzes how transportation decisions distribute benefits and burdens along racial lines through exclusion from planning, localized burdens, and unequal mobility access. White noose: the ring of suburban opportunity surrounding racially segregated urban cores. Racism without racists: discriminatory outcomes produced by facially neutral technical criteria layered onto an already segregated geography.
Who is centered: African American bus riders in Oakland and the East Bay, and the civil rights plaintiffs who challenged MTC's funding decisions in Darensburg v. MTC.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access: MTC's per rider subsidy favored more affluent, mostly White rail riders over low income bus riders of color, and courts accepted this as a legitimate outcome of neutral technical analysis.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports both halves of the claim. It documents historically uneven mobility access rooted in de jure discrimination, and shows that even facially race neutral, seemingly participatory regional planning processes reproduced exclusion because minority communities' participation and race equity concerns hit real limits within MTC's decision making.
Gap or limitation: The analysis focuses on one metropolitan region and one legal case, and does not evaluate whether newer transit oriented development plans in Priority Development Areas will repeat or interrupt this pattern.
Quotable moment: "racism without racists" (p. 24).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds the section's exclusion claim in a landmark case, showing that race neutral transit funding formulas, layered onto a metropolitan geography built by decades of overt discrimination, can reproduce racial exclusion without any single discriminatory actor. It cautions that formally inclusive planning processes do not guarantee equity when minority participation hits structural limits.
Codesign/participatory method: Historical and legal case analysis, not the authors' own fieldwork, of the San Francisco Bay Area's Metropolitan Transportation Commission (MTC) inviting community advocates onto an advisory committee to review its 1998, 2001, and 2005 regional transportation plan equity analyses after Title VI complaints, plus MTC's separate Partnership Board, an advisory only body of transit agency and government representatives it relied on to justify funding decisions in the later Darensburg civil rights lawsuit. Drawn from Sanchez (2008), Cohen and Hobson (2004), and Public Advocates litigation reports.
What worked: Federal corrective action following Title VI complaints did force MTC to formally invite advocacy organizations onto the advisory committee reviewing its 2001 equity analysis, opening a door that outright refusal to involve advocates in 1998 had kept shut (p. 19).
What didn't work: Advisory committee members found the process consumed large amounts of activist time on mostly technical discussion while MTC accepted few of their recommendations, leaving one member to call it worse than a waste of time and conclude MTC could now simply say it had consulted the community (p. 20). MTC separately leaned on its advisory only Partnership Board, whose transit agency members felt pressured to acquiesce rather than risk offending a key funding source, to legally justify funding decisions the court still found had a discriminatory impact (p. 21).

Paper Title: Implementation science frameworks for active and sustainable transportation interventions with a focus on equity: A scoping review
Central claim: A scoping review of 26 studies finds implementation science frameworks exist for active and sustainable transportation interventions, but only nine explicitly address equity, and community engagement, partnerships, and funding operate as both facilitators and barriers to equitable implementation.
Key concepts or framework: Implementation science: the study of methods and factors that determine whether evidence-based interventions get adopted in practice. Barriers and facilitators: context-specificity, community engagement and participation, partnerships and collaboration, and funding; the same factors can enable or block equitable implementation depending on how they are handled.
Who is centered: The perspective of researchers synthesizing published frameworks; the traditionally excluded groups discussed, such as low income residents, ethnic minorities, and women, appear only secondhand through the reviewed studies.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access and flexibility for variable need: most frameworks were built for able bodied road users, and community engagement is often only nominal, with marginalized groups excluded or deterred from participating in complex infrastructure decisions.
Relevance to argument: Supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, showing that fair representation and participation is necessary for equitable implementation, yet the studies reviewed report groups being actively ignored or deterred by feeling they lack the expertise to engage with complex infrastructure projects, producing unequal power among stakeholders.
Gap or limitation: Only 26 of over 8,500 screened studies met inclusion criteria, and most frameworks that do address equity were developed for Western contexts, which the review itself notes may not transfer to other institutional settings such as China.
Quotable moment: "excluding some from participating bequeaths unequal powers among stakeholders" (p. 14, McCullogh et al. quoting Al-Sharari, 2022, p. 1316).
Synthesis paragraph: This review shows that even when implementation frameworks name community engagement as a success factor, marginalized groups are frequently excluded or deterred from participating, concentrating power among project proponents rather than affected communities. It supports the section's exclusion claim while cautioning that most equity-focused frameworks are Western in origin and may not travel well to other contexts.
Codesign/participatory method: Scoping review, not the authors' own fieldwork. Section 4.2.2 synthesizes community engagement and participation as a named implementation theme across many reviewed active and sustainable transportation studies. Cited processes include Koester et al. (2021) engaging students, caregivers, and community members for a walking school bus program, Adams et al. (2017a) consulting a local community group to select a project route with regular check ins, Bakker et al. (2018) framing citizen participation in cycling policy as both active involvement and education, and Bejarano et al. (2021) crediting community organizations and neighbourhood resident support for program coordination.
What worked: Continuous, ongoing engagement rather than one time consultation was repeatedly credited as a facilitator. Adams and colleagues' regular "checking in" with community program coordinators helped track how an intervention evolved (p. 11), and involving local communities was described across several studies as building ownership, social cohesion, and a sense of community (p. 11).
What didn't work: Disjointed communication about launch dates and follow up support decreased perceived buy in from parents and residents and worried school leaders in Todorova and colleagues' study (p. 11). Separately, traffic related concerns tied to car oriented planning prevented parent buy in to a school remote drop off program in Bejarano and colleagues' study, showing engagement can fail for reasons outside the process itself (p. 20).

Paper Title: Inclusive Mobility: Dismantling transportation injustice at the intersection of race and disability
Central claim: Transportation injustice is a product of systemic racism and ableism that compounds for people who are both Black and disabled, since public transit systems were built around an ideal rider who is economically secure, able bodied, and white. Dismantling it requires an intersectional, mobility justice approach centering the leadership of those most impacted.
Key concepts or framework: Transportation injustice: structural conditions that perpetuate inequities, discrimination, and exclusion based on disability, race, class, gender, and age. Intersectionality: overlapping social identities compound rather than simply add experiences of discrimination. Crip Mobility Justice: a framework prioritizing accessibility, interdependence, and abolition of policing alongside physical infrastructure.
Who is centered: Black people and people with disabilities in the United States, especially those holding both identities, whose transportation experiences are argued to be understudied.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access and flexibility for variable need: transit systems designed around an ideal rider formally exclude disabled people and, through redlining and highway placement, disproportionately under-serve Black communities.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports both halves of the claim. It traces mobility exclusion to slavery, redlining, and highway construction, and gives a concrete contemporary case: Maryland canceling the Black-serving Red Line to fund the whiter Purple Line without seeking input from Baltimore residents or community groups.
Gap or limitation: The authors note a dearth of evidence at the intersection of race and disability specifically, since disability studies tend to exclude race and race studies tend to omit disability, leaving this population understudied.
Quotable moment: "The administration did not seek input from the Department of Transportation, Baltimore citizens, or community groups on this decision" (p. 2).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds the section's claim in a concrete recent case, Maryland defunding the Black-serving Red Line for the whiter Purple Line without community input, while tracing the same exclusionary pattern back through redlining and highway construction. It argues dismantling this requires sharing decision-making power with Black and disabled communities as leaders, not only building accessible infrastructure.
Codesign/participatory method: None described. This is a policy commentary drawing on historical and secondary sources, not the authors' own fieldwork. It recommends, as a forward looking policy prescription, involving potential users at all stages of the transportation lifecycle including design and advisory boards, but names no specific process, participants, or outcome.
What worked: N/A
What didn't work: N/A

Paper Title: Inclusive and Accessible Transportation for All: Strategies for Integrating Equity in Transportation Research
Central claim: A literature review of transportation equity research finds that horizontal equity, equal treatment of similar groups, and vertical equity, prioritizing disadvantaged populations, remain inconsistently defined and measured across studies, and that clearer frameworks, better data, and more inclusive decision-making are needed to close this gap.
Key concepts or framework: Horizontal equity: equal treatment of individuals or groups with similar needs. Vertical equity: allocating resources based on differing needs, prioritizing disadvantaged groups. Accessibility indices and affordability metrics: quantitative tools used alongside community engagement approaches to assess whether a transportation system is equitable.
Who is centered: The perspective of transportation researchers synthesizing published equity literature and metrics, rather than the residents these metrics are meant to serve.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust: the review treats community engagement as one measurement tool among several, alongside accessibility indices, rather than as the mechanism through which communities hold real decision-making power.
Relevance to argument: A thinner fit than most sources in this section: this is a broad measurement focused literature review rather than a case study of participation or exclusion. It touches the unevenly distributed half by cataloging accessibility and affordability metrics, and gestures at the participation half only in its closing recommendation for more inclusive, community-driven decision-making.
Gap or limitation: The review draws on a single geographic context, and the authors acknowledge that transportation inequities and appropriate remedies vary substantially by density and region, limiting how directly its recommendations transfer.
Quotable moment: "Inclusive decision-making processes that involve underrepresented communities will ensure that their voices are considered" (p. 25).
Synthesis paragraph: This review is useful mainly as a map of how transportation equity gets measured, horizontal versus vertical equity, accessibility indices, affordability metrics, rather than as evidence of participation's role in preventing exclusion. It is included with that caveat: its value here is cataloging the measurement landscape the section's case studies push back against.
Codesign/participatory method: None described. This is a review of quantitative and analytical equity assessment tools (cost-benefit analysis, multi-criteria decision-making, Lorenz curves, GIS clustering, accessibility indices), not the authors' own fieldwork. Community engagement is named only in passing, alongside affordability metrics, as one category of approach other studies use, with no specific process, participants, or outcome described.
What worked: N/A
What didn't work: N/A

Paper Title: Is the medium the message? Exploring the intersection of social media and collective action in the San Jose Bike Party
Central claim: Interviews and field observations with the San Jose Bike Party, a monthly mass cycling ride organized via social media, find participants hold contested and often depoliticized understandings of the event as collective action, complicating claims that social media organizing democratizes civic participation.
Key concepts or framework: Prefigurative politics: enacting the change one advocates for through the form of the collective action itself, here temporarily claiming road space for cyclists. Virtual activism: activism organized through social media platforms, of contested lasting impact. Democratic divide: unequal ability to participate in a movement based on access to its digital organizing platforms.
Who is centered: San Jose Bike Party organizers and riders, interviewed and observed by researchers who themselves participated in the rides.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access: the ride route is posted exclusively on electronic platforms, so participation depends on social media access and literacy, and many riders described unclear or purely recreational motives rather than a shared advocacy purpose.
Relevance to argument: A thinner fit for this section's specific claim: the study centers a recreational social movement rather than an infrastructure planning process, and most participants did not describe SJBP as political. Its relevance is indirect, since the authors connect it to broader questions of equity, access, and inclusion in cycling infrastructure advocacy, without empirically testing that connection here.
Gap or limitation: The paper does not analyze whether SJBP has produced any actual change in cycling infrastructure, planning, or policy, and the authors explicitly flag this as a needed direction for future research.
Quotable moment: "the ride route, which is exclusively posted on electronic platforms" (p. 10).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper is included as a boundary case rather than a direct source: it studies grassroots cycling collective action, not infrastructure planning, and finds participants' political motives were often muddled rather than clear. Its value to the section is the authors' own gesture toward equity focused cycling infrastructure advocacy, a connection this study raises but does not test.
Codesign/participatory method: The authors' own method is qualitative fieldwork on the San Jose Bike Party (SJBP): semi-structured one on one interviews, about one to 1.5 hours, and two focus groups of five and six participants, with 21 riders total, plus researchers riding along as participant observers and conducting moving interviews mid ride, with field notes and video. This studies a grassroots social movement's own culture, not an agency led consultation of residents. Substantively, SJBP itself pre plans rides and shares information with members beforehand, unlike the structureless Critical Mass rides it grew out of.
What worked: Riding along as participant observers, not just interviewing afterward, let researchers conduct interviews on the move and capture the event's atmosphere directly, yielding thick descriptions a seated interview alone would have missed (p. 8). The hour plus, semi structured format gave riders room to describe unclear or personal motives in their own terms rather than fitting a predetermined political frame (p. 9).
What didn't work: This is a study of a self organizing bike collective's own culture, not an evaluation of an agency's consultation process, so it offers no direct evidence on institutional participation succeeding or failing. The closest finding is methodological: participants themselves were often unclear or contradictory about what Bike Party represents, so the interviews surfaced ambiguity in collective purpose rather than a clean account of shared goals (p. 9).

Paper Title: Achieving transportation equity: Meaningful public involvement to meet the needs of underserved communities
Central claim: Despite civil rights and environmental justice mandates, transportation planning continues to disproportionately burden low income and minority communities because public involvement processes rarely give residents real influence over decisions. The paper proposes a three step model: community led identification of needs, dedicated funding to meet them, and community derived metrics to track progress.
Key concepts or framework: Just process versus just outcomes: meaningful involvement of historically burdened communities versus fair distribution of benefits and burdens. Priority unmet needs: a model of equity grounded in what communities themselves identify as needed, not abstract quantitative equity analysis. Participatory budgeting: dedicating funds directly to needs identified through community deliberation.
Who is centered: Low income and minority residents of the San Francisco Bay Area and California communities affected by MPO transportation planning decisions.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust and equitable access: standard MPO public involvement and quantitative equity analyses omit race and rely on distant forecasts, so they rarely translate community input into funded action.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. It argues traditional public involvement is a near absence of meaningful engagement, and proposes a concrete alternative in which community identified needs receive dedicated funding, directly linking genuine participation to just infrastructure outcomes rather than treating them as separate.
Gap or limitation: The model's case studies are drawn from California, a state with an unusually strong environmental justice advocacy history and well resourced community based organizations, which the authors note may limit transferability elsewhere.
Quotable moment: "a near-absence of meaningful public involvement through which affected residents can influence and shape decisions" (p. 2 of the author preprint).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers the section's participatory alternative in concrete, actionable form: community identified needs tied to dedicated funding and community derived metrics, rather than public involvement as a box checking exercise. It reinforces that meaningful participation and just outcomes are not separable goals, directly grounding the exclusion half of the claim in an implementable model.
Codesign/participatory method: Literature review plus two California case studies, not the authors' own fieldwork. CARB's SB 535 guidance process gathered community defined priority needs from community based organizations via public meetings and online input to shape statewide cap and trade investment criteria. Separately, the 6 Wins for Social Equity coalition, over 20 Bay Area social, economic and environmental justice groups, ran its own community driven process entirely outside MTC's official channels to build an alternative regional transportation and land use scenario, Equity Environment and Jobs, later formally analyzed by the agency alongside its own alternatives.
What worked: Advocates called CARB's engagement well executed and responsive during guideline development, and the process surfaced community defined needs, public health, safety, economic, and environmental, that diverged sharply from agencies' usual cost effectiveness metrics (p. 9-10). The 6 Wins coalition's self built EEJ scenario outperformed MTC's own alternatives on displacement risk, rent savings, and pollution, and the agency officially designated it the environmentally superior alternative among five scenarios (p. 12).
What didn't work: Community groups flagged that CARB's later individual project selection relied on posting information mainly online, creating a digital divide, and that no comprehensive evaluation of SB 535 public involvement has been conducted (p. 10-11). Despite the EEJ scenario's superior performance, MTC adopted only some of its amendments rather than the community's plan itself, so authorship of a winning alternative did not translate into full authority over the final decision (p. 12).

Paper Title: Limitations of Technical Approaches to Transport Planning Practice in Two Cases: Social Issues as a Critical Component of Urban Projects
Central claim: Case studies of Amsterdam's North-South Metro line and Sydney's Parramatta Rail Link find that technical, model driven transport planning consistently overlooks social impacts, contributing to lost social licence, poor communication, and inadequate protection of affected communities. Social Impact Assessment, applied early, offers a path to better integrate social issues into megaproject planning.
Key concepts or framework: Social Impact Assessment: a framework for anticipating and managing how projects change people's lives, distinct from purely economic or engineering impact models. Social licence to operate: a community's ongoing acceptance of a project, lost through poor communication and unmet commitments. Predict and provide: a quantitative, model driven planning approach criticized for ignoring wider social context.
Who is centered: Communities affected by two rail megaprojects, and infrastructure impact assessment practitioners interviewed about planning practice in Amsterdam and Sydney.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust and flexibility for variable need: technical, model driven planning treats social impacts as secondary to economic and engineering considerations, so affected communities' actual needs go unconsidered until consultation happens too late to shape decisions.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. Both rail megaprojects show that public consultation occurring late in the project lifecycle fails to transfer community input into how social impacts get assessed and managed, diluting the public's capacity to meaningfully shape infrastructure that affects them.
Gap or limitation: The study examines only two rail megaprojects in wealthy, high capacity planning contexts, Amsterdam and Sydney, so it may understate the barriers to adopting Social Impact Assessment in lower resourced planning systems.
Quotable moment: "dilute the capacity of the public to contribute meaningfully to transport planning" (p. 15).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper shows, through two concrete megaproject cases, that consultation without a mechanism to feed into actual project design amounts to participation in name only. It reinforces the exclusion claim by tracing the same failure, technical dominance sidelining community input, across two different high income cities, and proposes Social Impact Assessment as a structural fix rather than a procedural add on.
Codesign/participatory method: The authors' own method is roughly 30 semi-structured interviews with project stakeholders, government officials, consultants, aldermen, and citizens' representatives, across two infrastructure megaprojects, Sydney's Action for Transport plan and Amsterdam's North South metro line (NZL), plus a focus group with five impact assessment experts, analyzed thematically. The paper compares each country's formal consultation requirements within environmental and social impact assessment and land use planning against how much influence residents actually had over the final design.
What worked: Focus group experts and the authors agree that engaging communities early, during strategic and pre-feasibility assessment before the project concept is fixed, offers the greatest potential to build trust and genuinely incorporate alternatives that benefit local communities (p. 11). When impact assessment is treated as big picture thinking before action rather than a narrow legal box to check, practitioners say its role in shaping decisions can be substantial rather than just validating a plan already chosen (p. 11).
What didn't work: In Amsterdam's formally required citizen consultation, the plan was already finalized before residents were asked for input, and suggested changes were rejected as already decided, leading one citizens' representative to ask, "So why then do you ask us?" (p. 10). The authors read this as producing underlying public mistrust in the municipality and a lack of real influence over decisions, since formal consultation carried no requirement to actually modify the project.

Paper Title: Lived expertise of the structurally disadvantaged: towards a more just participatory transport planning process
Central claim: Focus groups with mobility disabled people and low income women in Berlin's Graefekiez neighborhood find that non-participation in street space reallocation planning stems from feeling excluded and ignored by prior participatory processes, while a purpose built, transdisciplinary research format better reflected residents' lived expertise.
Key concepts or framework: Lived expertise: the practical, embodied knowledge structurally disadvantaged people hold about their own mobility needs, distinct from technical planning expertise. Invited versus claimed spaces: participation opportunities designed by authorities versus spaces residents create themselves. Negative political self-efficacy: the learned sense that speaking up in official participatory venues will not lead anywhere.
Who is centered: Mobility disabled residents and women from a low socioeconomic status neighborhood in Berlin, recruited specifically for their structurally disadvantaged position.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust and equitable access: repeated negative experiences in official participatory venues, including public humiliation by a mayor, taught disadvantaged residents their input would not be acted on, so many stopped participating altogether.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. It shows concretely how invited participatory spaces, meant to democratize a car space reallocation project, actively discouraged the structurally disadvantaged residents they claimed to include, reproducing the same exclusion the project intended to fix.
Gap or limitation: The case study is a single Berlin neighborhood under a specific green party led local government, and the authors note it is not perfectly generalizable to other transport planning contexts.
Quotable moment: "I've been talking to and against walls for years" (p. 11).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers a vivid, first person account of how official participation processes can actively produce the disengagement they are meant to prevent, directly reinforcing the claim that infrastructure decisions without genuine participation reproduce exclusion. It also models an alternative, a co-designed research format residents experienced as more welcoming and reflective of their lived expertise.
Codesign/participatory method: The authors' own method is three rounds of two hour focus groups, August to December 2023, with mobility disabled residents and women from a social housing estate in Berlin's Graefekiez, recruited via flyers, social media, and visits to existing community spaces like a weekly women's breakfast, with a 50 euro allowance per session and a final round to collectively discuss findings. This studies the municipality's own Graefekiez street redesign participation program, which used mostly informative and deliberative formats, online surveys, flyers, information events, discussion hours, plus one collaborative parking redesign component, that participant observation found drew a mostly white, middle aged, non disabled crowd.
What worked: Locating focus groups within the neighbourhood and recruiting through trusted existing spaces, like the women's weekly breakfast, reduced physical and social barriers to participating in the authors' own research, though building the women's group still took much more relational work and time than recruiting mobility disabled participants (p. 8). A closing third round that returned findings to participants for collective discussion gave them a direct evaluative role in the research itself (p. 8).
What didn't work: In the municipal project itself, delayed information and outreach that skipped disabled and WDS residents' actual communication channels, newspapers and radio for one group, community social media for the other, left people feeling excluded before barriers like time, health, caretaking, or language even came into play (p. 9-10). Participants who had engaged with prior local processes described feeling ignored despite attending, one saying local politics amounted to a "friendly side offer" where "nothing fundamental could be decided" (p. 12).

Paper Title: Mindsets and actions: Shifts in equitable and sustainable development in U.S. cities
Central claim: Interviews with 23 urban development professionals across U.S. cities find a shift toward more explicitly equitable practices, driven less by government initiative than by community-based organizations and residents adopting radical demands for redistributed resources, alongside strategic framing to counter opposition rooted in individualist and racialized cultural mindsets.
Key concepts or framework: Bottom-up transformation: resident and CBO led initiatives that go beyond procedural inclusion to shift actual resource distribution and power. Bootstraps narrative: a cultural myth of unconstrained individual mobility used to oppose equitable investment. Tactical urbanism: temporary, small scale interventions, such as youth-led road redesigns, used to demonstrate what permanent infrastructure change could look like.
Who is centered: Senior professionals in community development, planning, transportation, and housing across U.S. cities, primarily in local government and nonprofits, describing their own strategies.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Relational trust: city processes and regulations were described as stacked against transformative solutions, so community organizations often had to build parallel, informal coalitions to get equitable projects taken seriously by agencies.
Relevance to argument: A moderate fit: transportation is one of several urban development domains covered alongside housing and parks, not the primary focus. Where most relevant, a youth-led tactical urbanism project redesigning a high-fatality road, it shows infrastructure change becoming possible only after community-led action pushed a reluctant state agency, illustrating the participation half concretely though not exclusively about mobility.
Gap or limitation: The study relies on 23 interviews with professionals rather than the residents whose neighborhoods are affected, and the authors note a remaining knowledge gap about the cultural mindsets that drive opposition to equitable development in particular places.
Quotable moment: "this would not have happened" without the youth-led project, which "sort of elevated it for [the state agency]" and "showed what was possible" (p. 11).
Synthesis paragraph: This paper is useful mainly for its broader pattern, that community-led pressure, not government initiative, has been the main driver of recent shifts toward equitable urban development, with a concrete mobility example, youth redesigning a dangerous road, illustrating how bottom-up organizing can force infrastructure change agencies would not have pursued alone.
Codesign/participatory method: The authors' own method is 23 semi-structured interviews with professionals working on equitable, sustainable urban development across U.S. cities, planners, public health officials, chamber of commerce, affordable housing developers, purposively recruited, transcribed, and analyzed with deductive content and narrative analysis. Within their accounts, one concrete case stands out: state funding backed a tactical urbanism group that worked directly with young people to redesign mobility infrastructure on a road with high pedestrian fatalities, starting from a small grant and growing into a significant state funded street redesign.
What worked: The youth led tactical urbanism project is credited with unlocking state investment that a public health official said "would not have happened" otherwise, because the project "elevated" the issue for the state agency and "showed what was possible" (p. 11). Cross agency steering committees built around specific projects were separately called "one of the most important parts" of similar efforts, fostering collective responsibility across organizations (p. 11).
What didn't work: Professionals described community and nonprofit led efforts as having to work very hard against city processes and regulations stacked against transformational solutions, with one leader unprepared for how long it took to win city leaders' support for a community land trust meant to prevent displacement (p. 11). Interviewees also described the emotional toll of this work, feeling "raw" after public meetings and spending extra hours to reach outcomes a smoother process would have reached faster (p. 10).

Paper Title: Mobilising equity. Emerging evidence for integrating vulnerable communities
Journal or Proceedings: TeMA - Journal of Land Use, Mobility and Environment, 18(1), 95-112
Central claim: A literature review of global best practices finds that technology driven mobility solutions, such as MaaS platforms and accessible transit systems, improve equity for vulnerable groups only when paired with inclusive land use planning, affordable design, and active community participation, and that rural regions and non-elderly vulnerable groups remain understudied.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility-as-a-Service: a digital platform integrating multiple transport modes into one accessible interface. Intersectional mobility vulnerability: overlapping identities such as gender, disability, race, and economic status that compound transportation barriers. Digital divide: unequal access to the devices and connectivity that ICT-based mobility solutions assume users already have.
Who is centered: The perspective of researchers and policymakers reviewing global case studies; vulnerable groups themselves appear as subjects of the literature rather than direct participants in this review.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access and flexibility for variable need: most ICT mobility solutions are designed around urban, digitally literate users, leaving rural residents and non-elderly vulnerable groups such as ethnic minorities underexplored and often excluded by design.
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half by cataloging how rural regions and multiple vulnerable groups remain underserved despite smart mobility advancements. It touches the participation half more lightly, noting that engagement must go beyond consultation to active participation in planning, without providing its own case study of that shift.
Gap or limitation: The reviewed literature is itself urban centric with limited rural evidence and no longitudinal data, and the paper is a review of secondary sources rather than original fieldwork with vulnerable communities.
Quotable moment: "engagement must go beyond consultation, requiring active citizen participation in planning" (p. 15).
Synthesis paragraph: This review is most useful for documenting the uneven distribution half, showing that smart mobility technologies leave rural residents and several vulnerable groups behind despite their promise. Its treatment of participation is brief and aspirational rather than evidenced, so it complements rather than substitutes for the section's more direct participatory case studies.
Codesign/participatory method: Case study of a Berlin Pankow Kiezblock traffic calming initiative, analyzed by the authors through participation reports, focus group transcripts, and workshop documentation from a co-production process, not the authors' own fieldwork with residents. A civic initiative had already drafted 19 conceptual layouts before formal planning began. The process ran four formats across three neighborhoods: moderated neighborhood walkshops, thematic workshops and planning roundtables, online map based feedback tools, and targeted dialogue with local businesses on delivery and loading needs. Resident input was cross validated against traffic counts, video observation, and GIS crash heatmaps, then translated by planners into implementable designs.
What worked: Combining resident input with independent traffic observation let planners compensate for uneven turnout. In the lower engagement Gruene Stadt neighborhood, systematic traffic counts filled gaps left by weaker civic participation, while the high turnout Winsviertel produced detailed, well contextualized proposals (p. 4). Translating residents' ambitious asks, like full street closures, into a legally defensible package of selective modal filters and school street timing preserved core safety goals while demonstrating responsiveness, which helped stabilize support (p. 6).
What didn't work: Several of the most ambitious civic proposals, area wide modal filters and full street closures, exceeded what the district could enact under existing German road traffic regulations, forcing scaled back compromises (p. 6). Even empirically justified measures still met individual resistance from residents, particularly older residents worried about parking or navigation, showing shared data could not resolve disagreements rooted in values and interests, and that legitimacy required continuous negotiation rather than being automatically produced by participation (p. 6).

Paper Title: Mobility Injustice by Design
Central claim: Drawing on research into unhoused, disabled, and aging city dwellers, this book argues that mobility injustice is produced by everyday design choices, benches angled to prevent sleeping, high curbs, short pedestrian crossing signals, not only by policy, and asks who the built world is actually designed for.
Key concepts or framework: Exclusionary design: material and spatial choices, intentional or not, that curb the mobility of vulnerable groups. Mobility justice: a framework asking who has the right to move, treating autonomous mobility as a fiction sustained by hidden assistance and dependency. Design justice: extending questions of justice to the artifacts and spaces that afford or restrict movement.
Who is centered: Unhoused street sleepers, disabled and impaired people, and aging citizens, examined through the author's Exclusionary Design research project in Copenhagen and beyond.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access and flexibility for variable need: cities are described as built for able bodied, middle class, ordinary citizens, so street furniture and crossing timing are designed around that default and against unhoused, disabled, and aging users.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, reframing exclusion as encoded in physical design decisions, hostile benches, curbs, crossing timers, rather than only in planning process or funding. This entry draws only on the book's introductory chapter and bibliography, since the empirical fieldwork chapters were not included in the available preview text.
Gap or limitation: Only the introduction and bibliography were available in the extracted preview; the book's empirical chapters on unhoused, disabled, and aging populations, where the fieldwork evidence lives, could not be reviewed here and should be read directly for case level detail.
Quotable moment: "Who is the built world built for?" (p. 15, Jensen quoting Hendren, 2020).
Synthesis paragraph: This book pushes the section's exclusion claim down to the level of material design, arguing that hostile benches, high curbs, and short crossing signals encode exclusion into infrastructure independent of any single planning decision. Only the introductory framing was available here; the book's later chapters presumably supply fieldwork evidence for unhoused, disabled, and aging Copenhageners that would let this claim be checked against lived experience.
Codesign/participatory method: This PDF is a preview containing only front matter and the introduction chapter of a book, not its empirical chapters. It describes drawing on the "Exclusionary Design, Social Exclusion in Urban Space" research project at Aalborg University (2021 to 2024), which collaborated with Copenhagen's city government and local NGOs and used ethnographic fieldwork and concealed identity interviews with unhoused people to document how street furniture and urban design push them out of public space. The chapters that would detail this fieldwork's methods and outcomes in depth (Chapters 6 to 8) are not included in this preview extract.
What worked: Not discussed in the available preview. The introduction names the collaborative research design and its city government and NGO partnerships but the empirical chapters that would detail which engagement practices succeeded are not part of this extract.
What didn't work: Not discussed in the available preview, for the same reason: the empirical chapters covering the unhoused, disability, and aging fieldwork are not included in this preview extract.

Paper Title: Mobility justice and accessible public transport networks for people with intellectual disability
Central claim: A focus group of 16 public transport and disability advocacy practitioners in Victoria, Australia finds that Melbourne's privatized, splintered transport network creates cognitive access barriers for people with intellectual disability that no single service provider can fix alone, requiring network wide collaboration and inclusive participation mechanisms.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility justice: understanding mobility outcomes as generated at the intersection of transport systems and wider social circumstances, here extended to cognitive access. Splintered urbanism: fragmented, privatized transport governance in which competing operators communicate inconsistently. Performative research: a focus group method aimed at prompting collaboration and change, not just recording existing conditions.
Who is centered: People with intellectual disability as public transport users, represented in the focus group by disability advocacy organizations and a person contributing lived expertise directly.
Value foreclosed (community value left o: Equitable access and flexibility for variable need: existing disability access committees typically focus on sensory and physical impairments and often exclude people with intellectual disability, and advocates who do participate are frequently expected to contribute expertise unpaid.
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. It shows existing participatory mechanisms, access committees and reference groups, systematically underrepresent people with intellectual disability, and argues genuine inclusion requires network wide collaboration across privatized operators plus fair compensation for advocates' expertise.
